message.content:
You are an adversarial deep-tech investor. EXECUTION skeptic: can a tiny team starting with software today actually reach a sellable product? Attack capital needs, hiring, sales cycle, technical risk.
Default to skepticism; score 1-10 where 7+ means you would actually take a meeting. Thesis:
{
  "name": "OpenBeam (merchant OCI-MSA optical engine, non-TSMC)",
  "one_liner": "The multi-source UCIe-fronted optical engine the hyperscalers just standardized for — built on GlobalFoundries/Tower instead of TSMC, sold to everyone who isn't NVIDIA.",
  "wedge": "An OCI-MSA-compliant optical chiplet (UCIe electrical side, parallel CWDM WDM optical side, targeting the standard's path to 3.2Tb/s per link) fabbed on GF Fotonix (monolithic CMOS+photonics, proven with Lightmatter/Ayar) or Tower/OpenLight (integrated lasers), sold to custom-XPU programs — hyperscaler ASIC teams (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft via Alchip/Broadcom-custom/Marvell-rivals) and AMD-ecosystem players who need optical scale-up but refuse single-vendor lock-in on Ayar Labs or a Marvell subsidiary.",
  "why_now": "The OCI MSA (March 2026, founded by AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, OpenAI) explicitly standardizes a multi-vendor optical scale-up interface — hyperscalers created it precisely because they want second and third sources. Consolidation just deleted the independents: Celestial→Marvell, Nubis→Ciena, DustPhotonics→Credo, Enosemi→AMD. Ayar Labs is the only scaled independent chiplet vendor left, and it just joined NVIDIA's NVLink Fusion orbit — making a neutral alternative more valuable, not less. GF is hungry for anchor photonics customers post-AMF acquisition and will co-invest in enablement.",
  "market": "Optical scale-up is the genuinely enormous prize: CPO $8-10B by 2030, with the scale-up tier (GPU-to-GPU/memory) called 'a new market' by LightCounting and validated by Celestial's $3.25B exit and Marvell's claimed ~$10B addressable. A merchant engine vendor winning 2-3 hyperscaler custom-silicon sockets ships millions of chiplets: $500M-1B+ revenue potential by 2030-2032. This is the biggest TAM of any thesis here — and the hardest to reach.",
  "competition": "Savage, and mostly better-funded: Ayar Labs ($870M raised, NVIDIA/AMD/Intel all invested, NVLink Fusion member, 5-year head start); Marvell/Celestial (owns the AWS-adjacent custom-XPU channel); Broadcom (will offer OCI engines alongside its custom-ASIC business); Lightmatter (interposer approach, ~$12.5B IPO war chest); Intel's OCI chiplet program; plus TSMC COUPE gravitationally pulling the biggest customers to its ecosystem. You win only on the specific vector of neutrality + non-TSMC supply + OCI-native design — and only if hyperscalers' multi-sourcing rhetoric converts to purchase orders for a startup.",
  "moat": "Thin until a design win, then extremely thick: a socket in a hyperscaler XPU program is a 3-5 year committed ramp with co-developed test/packaging flows. Pre-win, the defensible assets are microring/WDM design IP that hits OCI specs on GF's process (nontrivial porting work others haven't done), laser-integration route via OpenLight/Tower that TSMC-ecosystem rivals lack, and the neutrality position itself.",
  "capital_intensity": "High — this is honest deep-tech fabless, not lean: $30-50M to a credible sampling chiplet (multiple full mask sets at >$500K each, 4-6 month cycles, packaging/test development, a 40+ person mixed photonics/SerDes team), $150-300M cumulative to production qualification. The Ayar fundraising history ($870M) is the realistic benchmark. Requires a strategic CVC (AMD, a hyperscaler, GF itself) by Series A or don't start.",
  "software_mvp": "This week: an OCI-MSA link-compliance and architecture-exploration toolkit — open-source models of the MSA's UCIe+WDM stack, letting XPU architects sweep engine configurations (wavelength counts, launch power vs the ~24.5dBm budget, ring tuning overhead at ~0.12nm/mW) against their bandwidth/pJ-per-bit targets. It builds relationships with the exact 10 architecture teams who will someday buy the chiplet, shapes the spec conversation, and costs nothing but engineering time.",
  "risks": [
    "Capital risk dominates: $150M+ before meaningful revenue, in a sector where crossover funding can evaporate with the AI cycle",
    "Hyperscaler multi-sourcing may in practice mean 'Ayar plus Broadcom,' never a startup — the MSA guarantees an interface, not a customer",
    "TSMC COUPE ecosystem lock: if the volume packaging flow standardizes on COUPE, GF-based engines fight uphill on cost/integration",
    "Talent war: microring DWDM + UCIe SerDes engineers are being paid NVIDIA money",
    "Timing: optical scale-up volume is 2028-2030 (Feynman-generation per SemiAnalysis); a 2026 start hits the window only with flawless execution",
    "Acquisition is the likely 'success' outcome, and post-consolidation the buyer list is short (Broadcom won't, Marvell/AMD/Credo already bought)"
  ]
}

- slack:channel-digest: Get a digest of recent activity across multiple Slack channels
- slack:draft-announcement: Draft a well-formatted Slack announcement and save it as a draft
- slack:find-discussions: Find discussions about a specific topic across Slack channels
- slack:standup: Generate a standup update based on your recent Slack activity
- slack:summarize-channel: Summarize recent activity in a Slack channel
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest); or when searching the Slack developer documentation for any topic (socket mode, the Events API, OAuth, manifests, Bolt).
- slack:slack-messaging: Guidance for composing well-formatted, effective Slack messages using standard markdown
- slack:slack-search: Guidance for effectively searching Slack to find messages, files, channels, and people
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation

input.rationale: The market is real and the neutrality/second-source logic is coherent, but this thesis flunks the actual test — a tiny team starting with software cannot execution-path its way to a sellable product here. By the thesis's own numbers it needs $30-50M before first samples and $150-300M before production qualification, with a mandatory strategic CVC 'or don't start.' The software MVP is a free open-source link-budget toolkit with no revenue model — a marketing asset, not a wedge — and there is no intermediate sellable product between it and qualified silicon in ~2029. The timing window (2028-2030 volume) requires credible sampled silicon by late 2027, which from a 2026 software start demands hiring 40+ of the scarcest engineers in semiconductors and surviving 2-3 mask spins with zero slack. Hyperscaler procurement will fail a Series A startup on supply-chain risk before evaluating the photonics, and post-consolidation the acquirer bench is nearly empty. The write-up is admirably honest — its own risks section is the best argument against funding it.
fatal_flaws: Capital wall contradicts the premise: $30-50M to first samples and $150-300M to qualification means the 'tiny team starting with software' framing is fiction — the software phase generates zero revenue and de-risks none of the silicon, packaging, or laser-integration work that consumes the capital.

Software MVP has no conversion mechanism: an open-source OCI link-compliance simulator competes with hyperscalers' internal tools, commercial EDA (Ansys/Synopsys), and reference models the MSA members (AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA) will publish themselves; it earns meetings, not purchase orders, and nothing about it is sellable.

Timing is self-refuting: 2028-2030 volume ramp requires reliability-proven samples (laser FIT data, ring tuning over temperature, KGD test flows) by ~late 2027 — impossible from a 2026 standing start that must first raise a mega-seed, hire a 40+ person team from a talent pool of a few hundred locked-up engineers, and complete multiple 4-6 month mask cycles without a single slip.

Chicken-and-egg on the customer: hyperscaler XPU sockets are 3-5 year committed ramps and their supplier-risk reviews disqualify balance-sheet-thin startups; 'multi-sourcing' in practice means Ayar plus Broadcom plus maybe Intel — established vendors — a risk the thesis itself concedes ('the MSA guarantees an interface, not a customer').

Exit backstop is broken: the thesis admits acquisition is the realistic success outcome, yet Marvell (Celestial), AMD (Enosemi), Credo (DustPhotonics), and Ciena (Nubis) already bought, and Broadcom builds in-house — the failure mode is not acquihire, it's zero.
improvements: Invert the wedge into a paid product: sell OCI-MSA compliance/interop test IP, verification suites, and characterization services (the PCI-SIG/UNH-IOL model) — every MSA implementer needs conformance testing, it generates revenue in 2026-2027, and it earns the same architecture-team relationships without a $50M mask-set bet.

Make the strategic anchor a precondition, not a Series A hope: do not incorporate the chiplet plan until GF or a hyperscaler has signed a funded joint-development agreement (NRE-paid, capacity-committed) — GF's claimed hunger for anchor photonics customers is testable in one quarter of BD conversations.

Name the team or kill the thesis: this only works founder-led by a principal from Ayar/Celestial/Intel-OCI with a hyperscaler co-design relationship already in hand; a software-first generalist team has zero path to the 40 required photonics/SerDes hires.

Consider the narrower, cheaper beachhead: license microring/WDM macro IP ported to GF Fotonix (an IP-licensing business, ~$10-15M scale) to the custom-ASIC houses (Alchip, Marvell rivals, Broadcom-custom competitors) rather than fielding a full merchant chiplet — thinner margins but reachable by a small team, and it builds the same design-win option.

Stress-test the why-now against the counterfactual: if the OCI MSA truly creates second-source demand, Intel's OCI program and Broadcom fill it first; quantify why a hyperscaler would qualify a startup engine instead of dual-sourcing two incumbents before spending a dollar.
